clue.text: Drink tea with right university person? Indeed!

parts.note: cha is slang for tea
R = right
a don is a university teacher
nay in its old sense of 'indeed, what is more'

explanation.surface: Someone takes tea with a well-connected academic and is suitably impressed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drink tea' reads as a verb and its object, but Drink is the definition and tea starts the wordplay. NAY here is the emphatic 'and more than that', not 'no'.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by category: the answer is one particular white wine, and a wine is one kind of drink.

clue.text: Important official translation of icon's memoirs

indicators.note: translating turns the letters into a new arrangement

parts.note: anagram fodder, 12 letters including the S of the possessive

explanation.surface: A celebrity's autobiography is being translated for a foreign edition.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe S counts as a letter of the fodder, which is easy to miss.
explanation.definitionFit: A commissioner is a senior official in charge of a department or body.

clue.text: Included as part of exam on genetics

definitions.note: 'Included' works as 'among' in the sense 'counted in with': 'included were ...' / 'among them were ...'

indicators.note: the answer is literally part of the following words

parts.note: the letters run from the third letter of exam, through on, to the first letter of genetics

explanation.surface: A student notes which topics appear on a genetics exam.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer spans three words: ex(AM ON G)enetics.
explanation.definitionFit: A loose preposition-for-participle swap: 'the items included were...' and 'among the items were...' say the same thing.

clue.text: Diddle English female

parts.note: to do someone is to cheat them
E = English

explanation.surface: An Englishwoman is being swindled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'English female' reads as one phrase, but English only supplies E; female alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by category: the word names the female of deer, rabbits and hares, so 'female' is a broad stand-in.

clue.text: Tortilla chips, exotic nosh a Conservative tucks into

indicators.note: tucks into means the letter is slipped inside the rearranged food letters
exotic means strange or foreign, so the letters of nosh and a are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A Tory politician tucks into some foreign grub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tucks into' looks like eating, but it puts C inside NAHOS, the rearranged NOSH A.
explanation.definitionFit: Nachos are Mexican snacks of fried tortilla pieces, usually topped with cheese.

clue.text: Strangely use mag repeatedly — activity that should be avoided

indicators.note: strangely means oddly arranged, so the letters are reworked

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: repeatedly here means the word mag is used twice

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Reading the same magazine over and over is a pastime best avoided.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strangely' scrambles USE plus MAG twice.
explanation.definitionFit: A mug's game is a pointless pursuit only a fool would take on, so wise people steer clear.

clue.text: Minimal cover? Two-wheeler, not fully insured — not ideal at first

indicators.note: not fully means the word for the cycle is cut short of its final letter

parts.note: a bike is a two-wheeled vehicle

indicators.note: at first means the opening letters of the words before it

parts.note: first letters of insured, not and ideal

explanation.surface: A cyclist is only partly insured, a skimpy level of cover that is far from ideal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not' looks like it negates 'ideal', but it is one of the three words whose first letters are taken.
explanation.definitionFit: A bikini is a very small two-piece swimsuit, so it covers the body as little as possible.

clue.text: One breaking rules errs — art songs need rewriting

indicators.note: the letters are to be written out again in a new order

parts.note: anagram fodder, 12 letters

explanation.surface: A composer admits a mistake and says the art songs need rewriting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Errs' looks like the verb of the sentence, but it is part of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A transgressor is someone who breaks a law or rule.

clue.text: Get right away from ill-tempered animal

parts.note: morose = sullen
R = right, removed

explanation.surface: Advice to keep well clear of a bad-tempered beast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get right away' reads as 'flee completely'; here right is R, taken out of MOROSE.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by category: the answer is the largest species of deer, and 'animal' is the broad class it belongs to.

clue.text: Old news announcer welcoming Open University messenger

parts.note: a town crier called out the news
the initial letters of Open University, the UK distance-learning university

explanation.surface: A veteran broadcaster greets a delivery from the Open University.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old news announcer' suggests a retired broadcaster, but it is a town crier, who shouted public announcements in the street.
explanation.definitionFit: A courier carries messages or parcels.

clue.text: Cleverly innovative, one using idea at the outset differently

indicators.note: take the first letter of idea

parts.note: first letter of idea, added to the fodder

indicators.note: arrange the letters differently

parts.note: anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A description of an inventor who approaches ideas in an original way.
explanation.walkthrough: The fodder is 'one using' plus the I from idea; the whole surface reads as praise, hiding the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Ingenious means clever and original in design.

clue.text: Means of identifying someone in call beginning to play dead

parts.note: to call someone something is to name them

indicators.note: take the first letter of play

parts.note: first letter of play
the late X = the dead X

explanation.surface: Someone on a phone call is told to play dead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' is a link here, not a container instruction: the pieces simply follow each other.
explanation.definitionFit: A nameplate on a door or desk shows who is there.

clue.text: Somewhere to stay initially is needed now

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the start of each word is used

parts.note: I-s N-eeded N-ow

explanation.surface: A traveller urgently needs a place to stay.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one plea; 'initially' sits between definition and fodder and belongs to the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: An inn offers rooms for travellers.

clue.text: Dishonest scheme interrupted by resistance — get out fast!

parts.note: a scam is a swindle
R = resistance in physics

explanation.surface: A fraud meets resistance, and the crook shouts to the gang to flee.
explanation.walkthrough: R for resistance comes from physics, where it is the symbol in Ohm's law.
explanation.definitionFit: Scram! is a slangy order to leave at once.

clue.text: Keep in mind tips from expert in wet weather

indicators.note: in means the extreme letters are placed inside the weather word

parts.note: rain is wet weather

indicators.note: tips from means the two end letters of the word expert

parts.note: first and last letters of expert

explanation.surface: Remember the expert's advice when it is raining.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tips' looks like advice, but it means the ends of EXPERT.
explanation.definitionFit: To retain facts is to remember them, holding them in the memory.

clue.text: Getting rid of levying money for Government? No opening for that!

indicators.note: 'that' points back to the word just clued, and giving it no opening means its first letter goes

parts.note: taxing = levying money for the state; T removed

explanation.surface: A protester rejects a new tax outright.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No opening for that!' sounds like a flat refusal; it tells you to drop the T of TAXING.
explanation.definitionFit: Figurative synonym: taking an axe to jobs or schemes is headline slang for scrapping them.

clue.text: Maybe split second's importance

definitions.meaning: 'maybe' marks a split second as one example of a brief instant
the older sense of weight or significance, as in 'of great ...'

explanation.surface: A remark on how much can turn on a single instant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maybe' marks the split second as an example of a moment. The less common sense, moment = importance, lives on in 'momentous'.
explanation.definitionFit: A moment is a brief time, and also weight or significance.

clue.text: Not permitted in public

definitions.meaning: banned or off the table, as in 'smoking indoors is ...'
known to everyone, as in 'the secret is ...'

explanation.surface: A rule banning something in public places.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase reads as one rule, but it splits into two separate meanings of OUT.
explanation.definitionFit: Out means both ruled out and out in the open.

clue.text: Out of order, moped near walking area

indicators.note: the letters are not in their proper order

parts.note: anagram fodder, 9 letters

explanation.surface: Someone complains about a scooter parked by a pedestrian area.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out of order' reads as a complaint about bad behaviour; it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A promenade is a paved walkway, often along a seafront.

clue.text: Guardian's fury as side finally changes

indicators.note: finally changes means the last letter of the fury word is swapped for another

parts.note: anger means fury or rage
L, for left, is one side; it replaces R, right, the other side

explanation.surface: A guardian's rage when a team ends up switching sides.
explanation.walkthrough: The last letter of ANGER is R, right; 'side' changes it to the other side, L for left.
explanation.definitionFit: A guardian angel is a spirit believed to protect a person, so angel can mean a protector.

clue.text: Regularly visited, seems I have high opinion of country!

indicators.note: only every other letter is called on

parts.note: s-E-e-M-s-I: every second letter
to rate someone is to think highly of them

explanation.surface: A tourist, having visited often, declares admiration for the country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Regularly visited' sounds like a travel habit; it picks alternate letters of 'seems I'.
explanation.definitionFit: An emirate is a state ruled by an emir, such as Qatar or Kuwait.

clue.text: Spurious attempt to return on board bus

indicators.note: OG gets on board, inside BUS

parts.note: holds OG between B and US

indicators.note: to return is to go back, so the word is read back to front

parts.note: have a go = make an attempt

explanation.surface: A passenger makes a feeble attempt to get back on a bus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spurious attempt' reads as one phrase, but Spurious alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: both describe something false passed off as genuine.

clue.text: See you later in Derby? Excellent!

indicators.note: the answer sits in the next words

parts.note: the last two letters of Derby and the first of Excellent

explanation.surface: Someone asks if they will meet in Derby, a city in the English Midlands.
explanation.walkthrough: Der(BY E)xcellent: the question mark splits the hidden letters across a break in the sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: Bye is a casual farewell, like see you later.

clue.text: Irish footballer George by wine store, it's said, in book bought by many

parts.note: George Best, the Northern Irish Manchester United winger

indicators.note: the word is spoken, so only its sound counts

parts.note: a cellar stores wine

explanation.surface: A biography of footballer George Best, famous for his drinking, is a big hit.
explanation.walkthrough: George Best was a 1960s Manchester United star whose heavy drinking was notorious, which makes the wine store fit the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A bestseller is a book that sells in large numbers.
